enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (40 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (12 marks); Expression (16 marks); Accuracy (12 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write on from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity (e.g. your name, school, parentage etc). You should write between 450 - 500 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **c)** You have been accused of a crime you did not commit. Describe the situation stating what happened, why you were accused and how you were set free.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: the morning when the school money disappears.
2. What happened: the narrator is called to the principal's office.
3. Why accused: he was near the office on Friday evening and his fees were overdue.
4. How set free: he recalls seeing the gardener with a black bag and the principal checks it.
5. Conclusion: public apology and the lesson that truth comes out.

**Model composition (494 words)**

It was a Monday morning in the second term when my life changed suddenly. I was in Form Five, and I was known in school as a quiet and hard-working student. I had just arrived in the compound when the school bursar, Mr Ndi, came out of his office looking worried. Ten thousand francs, part of the class fees which he had collected on Friday, had disappeared from his drawer.

By the time the first bell rang, rumours were running around the school. During the assembly, the principal called my name and asked me to follow him to his office. My legs trembled as I walked past hundreds of eyes. In the office, the bursar told the principal that a student had been seen near his door on Friday evening, after classes. That student, he said, was me.

It was true that I had been near the office that evening. I had gone to ask the bursar for a receipt for my fees and, finding the door locked, I had waited for a few minutes on the bench outside and then gone home. Unfortunately, nobody had seen me leave. Worse still, my fees were slightly overdue, so people said that I had a reason to steal. I protested, "Sir, I did not take anything," but the principal only shook his head and told me to sit outside while he decided what to do.

For two days, I was treated like a criminal. Some classmates stopped talking to me, and others whispered when I passed. At home, my mother cried and my father asked me the same question many times, and every time I gave the same honest answer. On the third day, the principal informed me that the police would be called if the money was not found.

That evening, I could not eat. Then I remembered that on Friday, as I sat on the bench, I had seen the school gardener, Mr Fon, carrying a small black bag out of the staff block through the back door. At that time, I had thought nothing of it. Now it made sense. The next morning, I gathered courage, went to the principal and told him what I had seen, though I had no proof.

To my relief, the principal was a wise man. Instead of calling the police, he quietly asked Mr Fon to open his bag in front of the discipline master, the bursar and me. Inside was an envelope with the missing money. The gardener fell to his knees and begged for forgiveness, saying that his child was sick in hospital and he had been desperate.

The principal publicly announced my innocence at the next assembly and apologised for the suffering I had gone through. My classmates also came to me one after another to ask for pardon, and I forgave them gladly. That experience taught me that truth always comes out in the end, and that nobody should be condemned without proof.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 12 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 16 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 12 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Leaving out one of the three things the topic asks for (what happened, why you were accused, how you were set free).
2. An unconvincing release, for example the accuser simply changing his mind, with no event or evidence that clears the narrator.
